newsitem.title: THAILAND: Rescue plan lays bare Thai property woes.
newsitem.headline: Rescue plan lays bare Thai property woes.

text.p: The troubled Thai property sector faces a critical period as the spectre of bankruptcies among developers and in the finance industry has prompted the government finally to step in.
Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan has announced a rescue plan that could be worth as much as 70 billion baht ($2.8 billion) aimed at pulling the sector out of its three-year slump.

"I could not imagine the property sector in any worse shape. It has sunk to the bottom and it has no way to go but up," said Prapan Charuwattanachai, chief analyst at SITCA Investment and Securities Plc.
State-run Government Housing Bank said some 755,000 residential and condominium units were built in Bangkok and its suburbs during 1992-1996.
At the end of last year, the city had 350,000-400,000 unoccupied housing units, up from 166,237 three years ago. About half of the empty houses were in low-cost suburban condominiums.

Central bank governor Rerngchai Marakanond said on Tuesday the glut grew despite a construction slowdown which reduced the number of newly built homes to 70,000 units in 1996 from 130,000 annually in previous years.

Most analysts expected the sector to take a few years to recover. They said property projects were the main casualty of soaring interest rates and mortgage financing, which hit a five-year high of 13.50-14.00 percent in mid-1995 and have been at that level since.
They said high interest rates had choked off housing demand and crippled developers operating on small credit lines.
A report by property surveyor Jones Lang Wootton said the hit Bangkok condominium market would have a further 27,000 units by December 1997 and the number would rise to 33,455 by end-1999.

It said the property glut had put pressure on office rents. Average monthly office rents in the Sukhumvit and Asoke areas near the Bangkok central business district fell to 450 baht per square metre in mid-1996 from 480 at end-1995, it said.
Jones Lang Wootton said Bangkok's 5.93 million square metres of office space were expected to expand by 2.74 million in the next two years.

Finance Minister Amnuay's rescue plan called for the state-owned Government Savings Bank and the Government Housing Bank to loan up to 20 billion baht of concessional mortgage loans to civil servants buying their first homes.
The two banks will charge borrowing civil servants an 8-9 percent mortgage rate against the 13-14 percent levied by commercial banks.
Amnuay said the government would urge commercial banks to set aside up to 50 billion baht for taking over property projects with cash flow problems.
The creditor banks would be encouraged to launch a "Resolution Trust Fund" which would buy, at a 30 percent discount, cash-strapped but viable property projects.
Anant Kanchanapas, chairman of Bangkok Land Plc, welcomed the moves, saying they would help trim his company's backlog of 10,000 unsold suburban housing units worth 20 billion baht.
But Neil Semple of HG Asia Investment Research Ltd said: "The measures are unimpressive. It is not clear what they are trying to do. Normally good quality projects do not need help."
He said the best help the government could give the sector was to remove restrictions on free-hold land ownership faced by foreigners.
An analyst at Securities One Plc said, however: "This is the most serious, broad-based rescue effort that we did not see in the previous government."
He said developers would survive if they could weather hardship for another year.
(US$1 = 25 baht)
